sentences.text: Aurorazhdarcho was a relatively small pterosaur with a wingspan measuring exactly 537.8 millimeters based on the type specimen.
Fossil impressions reveal an elongated head with a high-positioned eye socket, a snout that may have carried a high rounded crest, and a relatively short neck showing signs of a throat pouch.
The genus is known from a single nearly complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions on a single rock slab, from which the counter-mold was removed.
It holds the distinction of being the oldest known azhdarchoid.
The name combines the Latin word 'aurora' meaning 'dawn' to refer to its antiquity with the genus name Azhdarcho, a mythical Kazakh dragon, while the type species name means 'first' in Latin.

The missing skull and neck elements are visible as impressions because their movement on the lake floor left a natural mold covered by organic remains, and subsequent swelling of the carcass may have caused the head to drift away.
The first to fourth wing finger phalanges have lengths of 119, 70.8, 50.8, and 50.6 millimeters, respectively.
The holotype specimen of Aurorazhdarcho micronyx is considered one of the earliest, if not the very first, documented pterosaur fossils ever found, likely unearthed between 1757 and 1779.
An adult Aurorazhdarcho fossil was uncovered in 1999 by amateur paleontologist Peter Kaszmekat in the Blumenberg Quarry near Eichstätt.
The species Aurorazhdarcho primordius was named and described in 2011 by Eberhard Frey, Christian A. Meyer, and Helmut Tischlinger.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as NMB Sh 110, was found in the upper part of the Eichstätt Formation dating to the early Tithonian of the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago.
Bennett suggested Aurorazhdarcho's interlocking teeth formed a basket for sieving food, functioning like spoonbill jaws for wading and catching individual prey.

The holotype specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved on a single slab, though it lacks the skull and neck because the animal died after a predator attack that nearly ripped off its head and neck.

Evidence suggests the animal died after a predator attack that nearly ripped off its head and neck, causing the body to sink quickly, and the individual was likely a subadult male indicated by fused ischiopubes and the absence of a wide birth canal.
The type species is Aurorazhdarcho micronyx, and synonyms include Pterodactylus micronyx von Meyer, 1856 and Aurorazhdarcho primordius Frey et al., 2011.

Originally, describers assigned Aurorazhdarcho to the superfamily Azhdarchoidea and placed it in a new family, Protazhdarchidae, of which it is the only named member, but Bennett in 2013 concluded that the genus is actually a ctenochasmatid based on analysis of specimens attributed to Aurorazhdarcho micronyx, considering its short neck and foot morphology.
Aurorazhdarcho lived during the early Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic in what is now Bavaria, southern Germany, specifically in the Solnhofen Limestone area of Eichstätt.
The time range for Aurorazhdarcho is from 149.2 to 145.06 million years ago.

Bennett concluded that Aurorazhdarcho primordius and Pterodactylus micronyx are the same species, treating primordius as a junior synonym of micronyx, while a 2025 study concluded that both Aurorazhdarcho primordius and Pterodactylus micronyx are junior synonyms of Gnathosaurus subulatus.

Describers rejected cladistic analysis, using comparative methods to find similarity to Ctenochasma elegans but concluding it belonged to Azhdarchoidea due to shared key adaptations, most decisively the low shoulder joint, even though the position of the shoulder joint in Ctenochasma could not be established and describers assumed it was high due to the close relationship of that taxon with Pterodactylus.
